questions.q: The Task API needs a full task, a create input, a patch and a summary. Why does the lesson derive them from one Task interface instead of writing four interfaces?
questions.explain: With four hand-written interfaces, someone adds priority to one and forgets the others. Computing types from one definition keeps a single source of truth.
options: When a field is added to Task, every derived shape follows, so they can never drift apart
Interfaces cannot have more than one version
Derived types are checked at runtime, hand-written ones are not

questions.q: What does type Settings = typeof defaults; mean?
questions.explain: In a type position, TypeScript's typeof means "the type of this variable". JavaScript's typeof x, which runs in the program and gives a string, is a different thing.
options: The type of the defaults variable, taken from its value

questions.q: With const defaults = { pageSize: 20, sort: "newest", showDone: false };, what is keyof typeof defaults?
questions.explain: keyof gives the union of property names. The value types come from indexed access: Settings["pageSize"] is number.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Each call returns a new object with one property replaced; defaults itself is not changed. The spread keeps the property order of the original.

questions.q: For function setting<K extends keyof Settings>(settings: Settings, name: K, value: Settings[K]) with Settings = { pageSize: number; sort: string; showDone: boolean }, which call does tsc accept?
questions.explain: K must be one of the property names, and Settings[K] ties the value's type to that name. showDone is a boolean, so true fits. The others use a wrong value type or a name that does not exist.

questions.q: keyof exists only for the compiler. What does this print?
questions.explain: At runtime you get the property names from Object.keys, the JavaScript way. name is just the string "sort", so defaults[name] reads that property.

questions.q: What is the type of STATUSES in const STATUSES = ["todo", "doing", "done"] as const;?
questions.explain: as const tells TypeScript the array never changes, so it keeps the exact values and positions. Without it, the type would be string[].

questions.q: With that STATUSES, what is (typeof STATUSES)[number]?
questions.explain: T[number] is "the type of any element" of an array type. For the as const tuple, that is the union of the three words.

questions.q: You forget as const: const STATUSES = ["todo", "doing", "done"];. What does type Status = (typeof STATUSES)[number] become?
questions.explain: Without as const, the array is a string[], because it might change later. Its element type is string, and the Status type stops protecting you.
options: string, so any text would count as a status

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: STATUSES is a real array at runtime, so it has a length and can be joined, looped over or shown in a dropdown. TaskId is number and Tag is string, but only for the compiler.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: as const only changes the type: the compiler treats the array as read-only, but nothing is frozen at runtime. Use Object.freeze if the runtime must enforce it.
questions.code:
const STATUSES = ["todo", "doing", "done"] as const;

console.log(Object.isFrozen(STATUSES), STATUSES.includes("done"));

questions.q: With type NewTask = Omit<Task, "id">, which is true?
questions.explain: Omit removes the listed properties from the type. So a client cannot choose its own id: { id: 99, ... } is an error. It is a compile-time check only; outside data must still be copied field by field.
options: NewTask has every property of Task except id, and a literal with an id is rejected

questions.q: What is Partial<Omit<Task, "id">>?
questions.explain: Read it inside out: Omit removes id, then Partial makes every remaining property optional. That is a patch: the client sends only what changes.
options: A task with an optional id and every other property required
Every property of Task except id, and all of them optional
Half of the task's properties, picked at random

questions.q: Which type has only the id and title of a Task?
questions.explain: Pick keeps only the listed properties; Omit keeps all the others. Pick<Task, "id" | "title"> is the lesson's TaskSummary.

questions.q: With type TaskPatch = Partial<Omit<Task, "id">> and status: "todo" | "doing" | "done", which line does tsc reject?
questions.explain: Every property is optional, so an empty patch is fine. But a property that is there must still have the right type, and "finished" is not a status.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Leaving dueDate out (undefined) keeps the old date. Sending null means "remove the due date", so it is copied. That is why the code checks === undefined and not ??.

questions.q: Why does applyPatch copy title, status and dueDate one by one instead of writing { ...task, ...patch }?
questions.explain: Types do not remove extra properties from outside data. Copying allowed fields by name is the fix for mass assignment you met in the user module.
options: The spread operator does not work with Partial types
A patch comes from outside; spreading it would copy any extra property a client sends, such as id

questions.q: What does const frozen: Readonly<Task> = { ... }; frozen.title = "Call Grace"; give?
questions.explain: Readonly<T> makes every property readonly for the compiler. Like all types, it does not freeze the object at runtime.
options: The title changes, because Readonly only affects id
A tsc error: title is a read-only property
A TypeError at runtime, because the object is frozen
Nothing happens, and no error is shown

questions.q: const labels: Record<Status, string> = { todo: "To do", doing: "In progress", done: "Done" }; What happens when you add "blocked" to STATUSES?
questions.explain: Record<K, V> needs a property for every key in K. So the labels can never fall behind the list of statuses.
options: labels stops compiling until you add a label for "blocked"
The new status is refused, because labels was written first

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: resolveOptions fills in a default for every missing option, which is what Required<ListOptions> promises: code that gets the result never has to check for undefined.
options:
In progress
{ pageSize: 20, sort: 'newest' } { pageSize: 5, sort: 'newest' }

In progress
{ pageSize: 20, sort: 'newest' } { pageSize: 5, sort: undefined }

questions.q: Why does resolveOptions(options: ListOptions) return Required<ListOptions>?
questions.explain: Required<T> removes the ? from every property. The function itself must fill them in; the type only describes the result.
options: So that callers must pass every option
After defaults are filled in, every option is present, so code that uses the result never checks for undefined
So that the options cannot be changed

questions.q: For async function loadStats(userId: number, includeDone: boolean) { return { userId, open: 3, done: 0 }; }, what is Awaited<ReturnType<typeof loadStats>>?
questions.explain: ReturnType gives what the function returns, a Promise of the object. Awaited removes the Promise, like await does.
options: Promise<{ userId: number; open: number; done: number }>
{ userId: number; open: number; done: number }

questions.q: What is Parameters<typeof loadStats> for that same function?
questions.explain: Parameters gives the parameter list as a tuple, in order. You can spread such a tuple into a call: loadStats(...args).

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The tuple [2, false] is spread into the call, so includeDone is false and done is 0. await gives the object whose type is Stats.

questions.q: With type Status = "todo" | "doing" | "done", what is Exclude<Status, "done">?
questions.explain: Exclude<U, X> keeps the members of union U that are not in X. It is a conditional type: U extends X ? never : U, applied to each member.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: email != null removes both null and undefined, but keeps the empty string, which is a real string. NonNullable matches: it only removes null and undefined from the type.

questions.q: What does the mapped type type Touched<T> = { [K in keyof T]: boolean } make?
questions.explain: A mapped type loops over the keys of another type, like for ... in over an object. For each name K it makes a property with the type after the colon.
options: An array of booleans, one per property
An object type with the same property names as T, each of type boolean
A copy of T where only boolean properties are kept
A function that checks whether T was changed

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Both title and dueDate have an error message, but only title was touched, so only its error is shown. Errors makes every property optional, which is why status can be left out.

questions.q: How is the built-in Required<T> written as a mapped type?
questions.explain: Inside a mapped type, -? removes the optional mark and -readonly removes readonly. ? alone adds the mark, which is how Partial is written.

questions.q: With type Unwrap<T> = T extends Promise<infer V> ? V : T;, what are Unwrap<Promise<number>> and Unwrap<string>?
questions.explain: A conditional type tests with extends. For a promise, infer V captures the inside type, number. A string is not a promise, so the "else" branch gives T itself. That is roughly how Awaited works.

questions.q: The lesson assigns wrong values on purpose, like const a: IsText<"hello"> = "other";. Why?
questions.explain: The error Type '"other"' is not assignable to type '"text"' reveals that IsText<"hello"> is "text". In VS Code you can simply hover over the name instead.
options: To test that the program crashes correctly
The error message names the type the compiler computed, so you can see it
Wrong values make conditional types faster
It is required before a conditional type can be used

questions.q: How many strings are in type EventName = `${"task" | "user"}.${"created" | "updated" | "deleted"}`?
questions.explain: With unions, a template literal type makes every combination: 2 entities × 3 actions = 6, from "task.created" to "user.deleted".

questions.q: With type ApiPath = `/${string}`, which line does tsc accept?
questions.explain: `/${string}` is any string that starts with /. "tasks" and "tasks/" do not, and 7 is not a string at all.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: There are two different event names, so the map has two keys. The second on("task.created", ...) adds to the existing list. The type EventName lists six possible names, but the map only holds what was added.

questions.q: With type Action = "created" | "updated" | "deleted", what is `on${Capitalize<Action>}`?
questions.explain: Capitalize makes the first letter upper case, for each member of the union. The other helpers are Uppercase, Lowercase and Uncapitalize.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: toPublic builds a new object with only the fields it lists by name, so the hash is not in it. That is what you want to send to a client.

questions.q: Someone rewrites toPublic(user: User): PublicUser as return user;. What happens?
questions.explain: A full User has every property a PublicUser needs, so it fits; extra properties are only refused in a fresh object literal. Types are erased, so the hash is still in the object. Build the public object by name.
options: tsc rejects it, because passwordHash is not in PublicUser
Omit removes passwordHash from the object at runtime
It compiles, and the returned object still carries passwordHash, which leaks to the client
It throws at runtime because of the extra property

questions.q: Why should toPublic list the fields to keep instead of copying the user and deleting passwordHash?
questions.explain: With "delete what to hide", a new secret leaks until someone remembers to delete it too. With "list what to keep", forgetting means a missing field, not a leaked secret.
options: Deleting properties is not allowed in TypeScript
Listing fields is shorter to write
It is safe by default: a secret field added later, like resetToken, is not sent unless someone adds it on purpose

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Nullable allows null for every property. ?? only replaces null and undefined, so the empty title stays '', while the null due date gets the fallback.

questions.q: Finish setting: return a new settings object with the property name set to value, without changing the original. The program should print { pageSize: 50, sort: 'newest', showDone: true }.
questions.explain: { ...settings, [name]: value } copies the settings and replaces one property; [name] is a computed key. The signature already makes sure value has the right type for name.

questions.q: Write the labels object with the type Record<Status, string>: To do, In progress and Done. The program should print To do | In progress | Done.
questions.explain: Record<Status, string> needs one label for each status, so a missing one is a compile error. STATUSES exists at runtime, so you can loop over it.

questions.q: Finish applyPatch: copy title and status only when they are in the patch, and copy dueDate when it is not undefined (null means "remove the date"). Copy by name; the extra id in the request must be ignored. The program should print 1 Buy oat milk todo null.
questions.explain: Spreading the task is safe (it is your own data); spreading the patch would copy the client's id: 99. Use === undefined for dueDate, because ?? would ignore the null.

questions.q: Write the type PublicUser (a User without passwordHash, using Omit) and finish toPublic so it builds a new object with the allowed fields listed by name. The program should print { id: 1, email: 'ada@example.com', name: 'Ada', role: 'admin' }.
questions.explain: Run the starter first: return user leaks the hash, and with Omit it would still compile. Only building the object by name removes the secret at runtime.

questions.q: Finish resolveOptions: fill in pageSize 20 and sort "newest" when they are missing, so the result is a Required<ListOptions>. The program should print { pageSize: 20, sort: 'oldest' }.
questions.explain: ?? keeps a given option and fills in the default otherwise. Because the return type is Required, forgetting a default would be a compile error.

questions.q: Write the mapped type Nullable<T> that allows null for every property of T. Then print the old database row's title and due date with fallbacks. The program should print (untitled) (no due date).
questions.explain: { [K in keyof T]: T[K] | null } keeps every property name and adds null to its type. Because the values may be null, the compiler makes you handle that, here with ??.

questions.q: Finish countByStatus: return a Record<Status, number> with how many tasks have each status, including 0 for a status no task has. The program should print { todo: 2, doing: 0, done: 1 }.
questions.explain: Start with every status at 0; the Record type makes sure none is forgotten. task.status is a Status, so counts[task.status] is always a known key.

questions.q: Finish eventName: join the entity and the action with a dot. The return type is the template literal type EventName. The program should print [ 'task.created', 'user.deleted' ].
questions.explain: A template string built from an Entity and an Action fits the template literal type `${Entity}.${Action}`. A typo such as `${entity}-${action}` would not compile.

questions.q: Finish toSummaries: turn each task into a TaskSummary, which has only the id and the title. The program should print [ { id: 1, title: 'Buy milk' }, { id: 2, title: 'Call Ada' } ].
questions.explain: Returning each full task would also compile, but the objects would still carry status and tags at runtime. Building { id, title } by name makes the runtime objects match the type.
questions.expected: [ { id: 1, title: 'Buy milk' }, { id: 2, title: 'Call Ada' } ]

questions.q: Finish openStatuses: return every status except "done", typed as Exclude<Status, "done">[]. The program should print [ 'todo', 'doing' ].
questions.explain: Inside the if, status !== "done" narrows status to "todo" | "doing", which is exactly OpenStatus, so push compiles.
